Connect the dots
Your machines are generating data you're not selling yet
IPercept's $16.5M raise isn't really about sensors — it's about the moment operators realized that utilization data, maintenance prediction, and member-engagement signals were sitting inside their equipment doing absolutely nothing. Every rep logged, every machine left idle at 6pm, every cable stack that spikes in March and dies in June is a business insight dressed as a hardware problem. The investors writing those checks aren't betting on Bluetooth — they're betting that the gap between 'we have machines' and 'we understand how our members use them' is worth serious money to close.
So what does that mean if you run a studio with twelve pieces of kit and no enterprise software budget? It means the question to ask your next equipment vendor isn't 'what's the warranty' — it's 'what data does this export, and where does it go.' Operators who start building that habit now, even manually with a simple utilization log, will have the baseline that actually makes smart tracking tools useful when they arrive. The infrastructure is coming. The data habit is the moat.
The rundown
01
$16.5M bet: IPercept wants to track every rep your machines make
Swedish startup IPercept just closed a $16.5M raise to put fitness machine tracking on the map — for operators, that's a signal that equipment intelligence is moving from nice-to-have to investment-worthy infrastructure.
Source: Tech.eu →
02
HFA's 2026 European Congress Is Bringing Fresh Industry Research
The Health & Fitness Association's European Congress is rolling out new industry research — and if you're running a studio or coaching business, this is the kind of data that actually shapes your next move.
Source: Health & Fitness Association →

The AI platform just closed a $3.5M raise to expand financial coaching and capital access for small business owners — if chasing loans and spreadsheets is your least favorite part of running a studio, this one's worth watching.
Source: businesswire.com →
04
HardScope launches a studio built around creator-led IP
The new media company is betting that fitness creators aren't just talent — they're the IP. For studio owners and operators, it's a signal that the creator-to-brand pipeline is getting a serious infrastructure upgrade.
Source: Variety →
05
Garmin snaps up Moxy Monitor—and 'Muscle Battery' is next
Garmin has confirmed its acquisition of muscle-oxygen specialist Moxy Monitor, with hints that a 'Muscle Battery' metric could be on the way. For coaches chasing the next edge in recovery and readiness data, this one's worth watching closely.

✓ Try: Run a one-page cash-flow forecast monthly, not quarterly — most studio operators discover late payment patterns and seasonal dips only after they hurt. A simple rolling 90-day view changes that.

The beauty-wellness merger isn't a trend — it's a land grab
Amaani just pulled in $5M led by BECO Capital to scale a brand sitting squarely at the intersection of beauty and wellness. That's not a niche raise — that's investors betting that consumers no longer separate 'feeling good' from 'looking good.' The spa menu, the skin-health consultation, the recovery ritual: these aren't add-ons anymore, they're the category.
For studio operators, the so-what is this: your four walls of treadmills and kettlebells are competing against experiences that address the whole self. You don't need a skincare line — but you do need to audit whether your client journey ends at the workout or extends into recovery, ritual, and results they can see. The studios that figure this out first won't just retain clients longer; they'll command higher ticket prices.

DAILY

— Sqwod
Money movement

Connect the dots
Churn or billing glitch? The answer changes everything.
There's a quiet disaster hiding in most studio dashboards: a failed payment triggers a lapse, the system logs a cancellation, and an operator spends the next quarter blaming their programming. But the member never actually wanted to leave — their card expired. That's not a retention problem; that's a collections problem, and those are much easier to fix.
The practical upshot: before you redesign your onboarding, slash prices, or panic-hire a community manager, pull your last 90 days of involuntary churn and see how many exits trace back to billing failures. If your payment recovery flow is a single automated email, you're leaving real members — and real revenue — on the table. A dunning sequence with 3–5 touches (email, SMS, in-app) can claw back a meaningful slice of what you assumed was lost.
The rundown
01
The Churn Problem Hiding in Your Failed Payments
Athletech News flags a sneaky revenue leak operators often misread as cancellations: failed payments quietly pushing members out the door before anyone notices. Fix the billing, and you might find your retention numbers were better than you thought.
Source: Athletech News →
02

Shareholders are voting on a full cash buyout of Jamieson Wellness at C$45.75 per share — a reminder that even the biggest names in the supplement aisle aren't immune to a quiet acquisition when the price is right.

Connect the dots
House rules are theatre until you enforce them publicly
When a Bengaluru member hurled 20-kg equipment and Cult Fitness cancelled their membership, the real product wasn't discipline — it was signal. Every other member watching (and the internet definitely watched) learned exactly where the line is. Most studios post rules on a laminated sheet and pray. The ones that enforce fast and visibly are building something more durable: a culture with actual teeth.
Here's the operator truth: your code of conduct is only as strong as the last time you acted on it. If your staff hesitated, escalated for thirty minutes, or quietly let it slide, you don't have a policy — you have a suggestion. Audit your incident protocol this week. Who has authority to act? What's the script? Because as the KPMG story proves, the internet will timestamp every second of your team's indecision and fundraise around it.
The rundown
01
DSSV takes fitness lobbying to the Reichstag steps
Germany's gym industry association staged a live workout outside parliament to put fitness policy on politicians' radar. If you've ever wanted proof that the sector is flexing its political muscle, this is it.

Bird&Be Pulls in $13M to Put Male Fertility on the Map
The fertility brand just closed a $13M raise to bring male reproductive health into the mainstream conversation. For wellness operators, it's a signal that men's health is moving from niche to necessary — and that's a market worth watching.

20-kg wake-up call: Cult Fitness boots member who hurled equipment

The UK startup just secured £8m to take its AI-powered mirror stateside — which means the connected fitness hardware race is still very much on, and the market you're competing in just got a little more crowded.

Connect the dots
AI coaching just raised $5.96M — what's your moat?
General Catalyst doesn't write $5.96M Series A checks for fun. Disha's raise signals that the smartest money in tech now believes AI can sit in the coaching chair — not just hand out macros, but guide, adapt, and retain clients at scale. That's not a distant threat; that's a funded competitor with no rent, no sick days, and infinite patience.
Here's the rep that matters for operators: AI wins on availability and data; humans win on accountability, culture, and the moment a client is about to quit. Your moat isn't your programming — it's the irreplaceable feeling that someone who knows them is watching. Audit your client touchpoints this week and ask honestly: which ones could an algorithm already do better, and which ones only you can own?
The rundown
01
$685M Bid: VivaGym's Owner Eyes Fitness Park Takeover
The group behind VivaGym is reportedly leading a $685M race to acquire Fitness Park. If a deal lands, it could reshape the European budget gym landscape — worth watching if you're operating in that market.
Source: Athletech News →
02
Disha Pulls $5.96M to Put AI in the Coaching Chair
General Catalyst just led a $5.96M Series A into Disha, an AI health coaching platform — a signal that big money is betting the next great coach might not need a whistle. If you're building or running a fitness business, the AI-assisted coaching wave just got a serious financial tailwind.
Source: Ventureburn →
03
One simple move to protect your clients' overhead strength
The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette spotlights a straightforward exercise that preserves overhead strength — worth filing away for any coach whose clients spend more time hunched over screens than pressing overhead.
Source: The Arkansas Democrat-Gazette →
04
$201 Apart: Is the Fitbit Air or Garmin Cirqa Worth It?
Geeky Gadgets put the Fitbit Air and Garmin Cirqa head-to-head — and that $201 price gap is the real workout. For coaches and studio operators kitting out clients or staff, knowing exactly what you're paying for (and what you're not) is the rep that matters.
Source: Geeky Gadgets →
05

Connect the dots
Chuze + reformers: boutique's competitive edge is leaking
Chuze Fitness rolling out reformer Pilates via iFIT and Freemotion isn't a gimmick — it's the clearest signal yet that high-demand boutique formats are being commoditised at scale. The playbook is familiar: budget operators watch boutiques validate a format, then absorb it at a price point independents can't match. Pilates just joined HIIT and cycling on that list.
So where does that leave you? Not competing on equipment access — competing on depth. Programming expertise, coach relationships, community rituals, and outcome tracking are the things a big-box floor can't replicate at $25/month. The operators who'll feel this least are the ones already selling transformation, not just reformer time. If your differentiator lives in the machine, it's time to move it into the room.

Record industry growth means nothing if your studio didn't grow
The 2026 HFA Global Report confirmed double-digit revenue growth across the fitness industry in 2025 — the kind of headline that feels great until you realize rising tides expose who's been swimming naked. If your numbers didn't move with the market, you weren't losing to a bad economy; you were losing to stronger operators in the same tailwind.
That's the uncomfortable gift of a record year: it strips away the 'tough environment' excuse and hands you a clear diagnostic. Pull your 2025 revenue against the industry benchmark. If you underperformed a double-digit growth market, the gap is your actual strategic problem — pricing, retention, programming, or visibility — and 2026 is the year to name it and fix it, not coast on the good-news headline.
